metaDescription: Six pour-over coffee makers compared by filter type, carafe material and size, from a classic glass Chemex to an OXO with a self-metering water tank.
expertTake: The Chemex 8-cup is the best overall pick because its thick paper filter gives the cleanest cup and the one-piece glass pot has no hidden parts. The Bodum 34-ounce is the value choice for anyone who wants a permanent filter and no paper. Anyone who wants a no-attention morning should skip manual pour-over and use an automatic drip machine.
introParagraphs: Pour-over brewing has no heater and no pump. You pour hot water in a slow spiral over a bed of grounds in a filter, and gravity pulls the coffee through into a carafe below. The brew depends on three things you control: grind, water temperature and the speed of the pour.

That control is the reason people like it and the reason some quit. The vessel you choose sets how forgiving the process is, from the filter material to the size of the carafe and whether the device meters the water for you. We ranked six pour-over makers on exactly those points.

products.name: Chemex Classic Series 8-Cup Pour-Over Glass Coffeemaker
products.description:
The Chemex is a single piece of non-porous borosilicate glass shaped like an hourglass. The upper cone holds the filter and the lower carafe holds the coffee, and nothing in the path can hold old flavors. The glass does not absorb odors, which is why it stays clean after years of daily use.

Its signature is the thick paper filter, which traps more oils and fines than a standard cone filter or a metal screen. The outcome is a very clean, bright cup, different from the heavier body that a mesh filter gives. The thickness also slows the drawdown, so it rewards a steady pour and a slightly coarser grind.

Compared with the Cosori, it is simpler and more elegant but needs paper filters and a gentle hand, since the glass can break. The maker notes that coffee can be covered and refrigerated for reheating without losing flavor. This is the one to buy if you value a clean cup and a durable design over convenience. A wooden collar on the classic series gives a safe grip when the glass is hot.
products.bestFor: Drinkers who value the cleanest cup and a classic design.
pros: One-piece non-porous glass holds no stale flavors
Thick paper filter gives a very clean cup
Eight-cup size serves two to four drinkers
Simple design with no parts to wear out
cons: Needs paper filters and a gentle pour
Glass breaks if knocked or dropped

products.name: Bodum 34 oz Pour-Over Coffee Maker with Steel Mesh Filter
products.description:
A glass carafe with a permanent stainless steel mesh filter that sits on top, so there is no paper to buy. The mesh lets coffee oils through, which makes a heavier cup than a paper filter yields. A cork band around the carafe gives a safe grip, since the glass can be hot.

At 34 ounces it is a good size for a small household. Compared with the Chemex, it is cheaper to run, and a little rougher in the cup. The steel mesh passes a small amount of fine silt, which some drinkers like and others avoid. The simple frame is easy to take apart and rinse.

Expect to wash the mesh after each use with a brush, since fine grounds clog the holes. Glass is the weak point, and the cork band can stain over time. Expect a good pick for someone who wants a manual brewer with no ongoing filter cost. Wash the cork band by hand and let it dry fully.
products.bestFor: Hand brewers who want no paper filters and a low price.
pros: Permanent steel mesh avoids buying paper
Cork band gives a safe grip on hot glass
34 oz size suits a small household
Simple parts are easy to rinse
cons: Mesh passes more silt than a paper filter

products.name: Cosori 8-Cup Pour-Over Coffee Maker with Double-Layer Steel Filter
products.description:
A double-layer stainless filter does the straining here. Two layers of 304 stainless steel hold back more fine grounds than a single mesh while still letting coffee oils through, which gives a full-bodied cup with less silt. The borosilicate decanter is rated for thermal shock.

The 34-ounce decanter fits eight 4-ounce cups, which is a convenient size for sharing. Compared with the Bodum, the filter is finer and more refined, and compared with the Chemex it avoids paper. The cost is cleaning: the double layer needs a thorough rinse after each use.

The maker says the decanter is thermal resistant enough to be heated gently on a stove, which gives some flexibility but is not a reason to risk it. Keep the filter clean with a brush and the cup will stay clear. Best suited to a household that wants a no-paper pour-over with a cleaner result than a single mesh. It also handles a small bloom pour well because of the wide cone.
products.bestFor: People who want a permanent filter with less silt.
pros: Double-layer 304 filter holds back more fine grounds
Keeps coffee oils for a full-bodied cup
Decanter fits eight 4 oz cups
No paper filters to buy
cons: Double layer takes more effort to clean
Glass decanter can still crack from impact

products.name: OXO Brew Pour-Over Coffee Maker with Water Tank
products.description:
This is the answer to the hardest part of pour-over, the pour. A tank on top meters water onto the grounds through a controlled drip, so you fill it, set it and walk away. A built-in timer helps you hit a consistent brew time, and markings on the tank show how much water to add, up to 12 ounces.

The tank limits it to a single cup or a small mug, which is a big difference from the 34-ounce Bodum and Cosori. It is smaller but far more consistent for a beginner, since the flow rate is set by the device rather than your wrist.

The tank needs rinsing, and the parts that meter water can clog if fine grounds get in. It suits a person who wants the quality of a manual cup with the effort of an automatic one. For two or more people, a larger brewer is more practical. The filters fit the cone only, so buy a matching size.
products.bestFor: Single-cup drinkers who want a consistent pour without a gooseneck.
pros: Auto-drip tank sets the pour rate for you
Built-in timer promotes consistent brews
Tank markings show how much water to add
Walk away while it brews
cons: Limited to about 12 oz per brew
Metering parts can clog and need rinsing

products.name: Melitta 42 oz Pour-Over Brewer and Thermal Carafe Set
products.description:
The set pairs a pour-over cone with a stainless steel thermal carafe, so the coffee stays hot after the brew without a hot plate. Paper cone filters are included, which gives a clean cup and a simple start. The cone sits on top of the carafe and you pour water in stages.

At 42 ounces, it is the largest pour-over on this list, which suits a couple or a small group. Compared with the glass models, the thermal carafe will not break and holds heat for hours, but you cannot see the brew inside.

The cone and carafe are easy to wash, and replacement filters are cheap and common. The paper filter holds back oils for a clean cup, so the flavor resembles a Chemex more than a mesh filter. Look at it as a sensible choice for a household that wants hot coffee for a long morning without electricity. If you want a larger batch, brew twice or pick a bigger carafe.
products.bestFor: Couples or small groups who want hot pour-over for hours.
pros: Stainless thermal carafe keeps coffee hot without a plate
Largest pot at 42 oz
Paper cone filters give a clean cup
Brewer, carafe and filters come in one set

products.name: Bean Envy 20 oz Pour-Over Glass Dripper with Steel Filter
products.description:
The Bean Envy is a compact glass dripper with a steel filter and a 20-ounce carafe. Three components are all dishwasher safe, which makes cleanup simple. The borosilicate carafe is rated for boiling water.

At 20 ounces it makes about two mugs, so it suits one or two drinkers. It uses a steel filter, so it gives a heavier cup than the Chemex, and a smaller footprint than the Bodum or Cosori. A smaller carafe also saves counter space.

Expect to clean the filter with a brush to prevent clogs, even if it is dishwasher safe. The carafe is glass and can crack if knocked. Expect a sensible choice for a small kitchen or an office desk where space is tight and you want an easy-clean manual brewer. It is also easy to pack for a trip.
products.bestFor: One or two drinkers who want an easy-clean glass dripper.
pros: Three dishwasher-safe parts simplify cleanup
Compact 20 oz size saves space
Steel filter avoids paper costs
Borosilicate carafe handles boiling water
cons: Only about two mugs per brew

buyingCriteria.explanation: Paper, as on the Chemex and Melitta, traps oils and fines for a clean, bright cup. Metal, as on the Cosori, Bodum and Bean Envy, lets oils through for a heavier cup with some silt. Choose by taste first. If you are unsure, buy a pack of paper cone filters and try one brew with each style before you commit.

Glass lets you watch the drawdown but breaks, as on the Chemex, Bodum and Bean Envy. A stainless thermal carafe, as on the Melitta set, holds heat and survives drops. Choose thermal if you drink over a long morning. Preheating a glass carafe with hot water before the brew reduces the chance of thermal stress.

The Bean Envy makes 20 ounces, the Bodum and Cosori 34, the Chemex about 40 and the Melitta 42. The OXO does a single mug. Brewing far below the filter's design volume gives weak, fast coffee. A smaller dose in a big filter spreads thin, so keep the coffee bed at a sensible depth.

Pour-over depends on the speed and pattern of your pour. The OXO tank meters water automatically, while the others need a steady hand and ideally a gooseneck kettle. A consistent pour matters more than a fancy brewer. Pour in stages, starting with a short bloom pour that wets the grounds and lets gas escape.

A medium-coarse grind and water just off the boil, around 200 F, suit most pour-overs. Too fine a grind slows the drawdown and over-extracts. A thick paper filter, like the Chemex, wants a slightly coarser grind. Weigh the coffee and water with a kitchen scale if you want repeatable results from day to day.

Paper filters go in the compost bin, while mesh filters need a brush. Dishwasher-safe parts, as on the Bean Envy, save time. Consider how much effort you will give each morning. A mesh filter that is rinsed straight away takes seconds, while one left overnight needs a soak.

specDecoder.meaning: Glass with low thermal expansion that survives hot water. It still breaks on impact.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Chemex, Bodum, Cosori and Bean Envy all use it. Pre-warming the glass keeps the brew temperature steady.

specDecoder.meaning: Two layers of steel mesh hold back finer particles than one. It gives a cleaner cup without paper.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Cosori has one, and the Bodum uses a single mesh. Brush it under running water, not just a rinse.

specDecoder.meaning: A tank that meters water onto the grounds at a set rate. It replaces the manual pour.
specDecoder.watchFor: The OXO has one and holds up to 12 ounces. The tank lets a beginner reach a consistent result in the first week.

specDecoder.meaning: Brewers rate cups at 4 or 5 ounces, not mug size. A 34-ounce carafe fits eight 4-ounce cups.
specDecoder.watchFor: Expect about three or four mugs from the 34-ounce models. Brew with a mug in mind, not the stamped cup number.

specDecoder.meaning: A double-wall stainless pot that keeps coffee hot without power. It avoids glass breakage.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Melitta set includes one. A cork band or sleeve is still needed on a plain glass pot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Filter design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared paper and metal filters for clarity and effort. The Chemex's thick paper scored highest for a clean cup, and the Cosori's double layer led the metal filters. We did not score flavor claims from the makers, only the mechanics of the filter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of the pour
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how forgiving each device is. The OXO's metered tank scored highest, and the others depend on the user's hand. A forgiving brewer lets a beginner get a good cup early on.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat holding
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared glass carafes against the stainless thermal carafe in the Melitta set. The thermal design scored highest for long mornings. Glass models lost a few points for losing heat on a cool kitchen morning.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 20, 34, 40 and 42 ounce capacities against typical households. A size matched to the usual batch scored higher than the largest. A mismatch between dose and filter size is the most common cause of a weak cup.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed breakage risk, filter cost and cleaning. Dishwasher-safe parts and replaceable filters scored higher. Replacement carafes and filters were checked where the listing mentioned them.

cards.label: Paper
cards.text: The Chemex and Melitta use paper filters that hold back oils and fines. The cup is clean and bright, and the filters are an ongoing cost.

cards.label: Metal
cards.text: The Cosori, Bodum and Bean Envy use steel filters that pass oils. The cup is fuller and a little silty, and there is no paper to buy.

howToChoose.note: Choose paper for clarity and metal for body and savings.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A device that meters water or forgives a poor pour, plus a filter that is easy to clean. Use a kitchen scale and a timer.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The OXO tank meters the pour, and the Bean Envy has three dishwasher-safe parts that are easy to clean.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You value the cleanest cup and a classic design. The Chemex offers both.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You want a no-paper pour-over at a low cost. The Bodum and Bean Envy do the job.

maintenance.why: Coffee oils harden in mesh and go rancid. A quick rinse with a soft brush prevents clogs. Hold it at an angle and use a small brush for the corners.
Oils film the glass and steel. Warm soapy water removes them. Avoid abrasive pads, which scratch glass and steel.
A used paper filter cannot be reused. Keep a spare stack on hand. Compost them with the used grounds.
A hairline crack can fail under hot water. Retire a damaged carafe. Check around the rim and the base.
Fine grounds can clog the flow path on tank models. A rinse keeps the drip even.

faq.a: It gives you control over grind, temperature and pour, which can produce a cleaner cup. An automatic drip machine is easier and more consistent for a large batch. For a single cup the effort is small, and for a crowd a machine saves time.

faq.q: Do I need a gooseneck kettle?
faq.a: It helps with a slow, accurate pour, but it is not required. The OXO tank meters water for you, and a steady hand with a normal kettle works for the others. A thermometer helps hit about 200 F.

faq.q: Which filter is better, paper or metal?
faq.a: Paper gives a cleaner, brighter cup. Metal gives a heavier cup and saves on filters. Try the one that suits your taste. Try a few brews of each before you decide.
A medium-coarse grind is a good start, about the texture of coarse sand. Too fine a grind clogs the filter and over-extracts. Adjust a little finer or coarser in small steps.

faq.q: Can I reheat coffee in a pour-over carafe?
faq.a: The Chemex maker says coffee can be covered and refrigerated for reheating. Use gentle heat and avoid reheating glass on a hot stove. Reheated coffee never matches a fresh brew, so brew what you will drink.

faq.q: Why does my pour-over taste sour?
faq.a: The water may be too cool, the grind too coarse or the brew too fast. Use water near 200 F, a finer grind and a slower pour. Adjust only one variable at a time.
